chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Yaqub ibn Yazeed, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from Abdul Malik ibn Qudama, from his father, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said one day to his companions: 'Do you know what is weakness (al-'ajz)?' They said, 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' So he said: 'Weakness is of three types: One of you hastens to prepare food for his companion, but he breaks his promise and does not come to him; and the second is that a man from you accompanies another man or sits with him, loving to know who he is and from where he is, but he separates from him before he gets to know that; and the third is a matter of women. One of you approaches his wife and fulfills his need, while she has not fulfilled her need.'
Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As said, 'So how is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said, 'He should hold back and wait until that comes from both of them together.'

He said, 'And in another hadith, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'From the most extreme of weaknesses is the weakness of a man who meets a man, is impressed by his manner, but does not ask him about his name, his lineage, and his place (residence).'

key_terms.أَمْرُ النِّسَاءِ: The matter of women (specifically marital relations)
key_terms.يَبْدُرَ: To hasten or be quick to do something

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of weakness (al-'ajz) mentioned in this hadith regarding social and marital conduct?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, this hadith defines 'al-'ajz' (deficiency/weakness) not as physical incapacity, but as social and emotional negligence, highlighting the Prophet’s emphasis on mutual respect in hospitality, companionship, and marital intimacy. The specific mention of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As provides a practical illustration of the marital aspect, urging patience and reciprocity to ensure both partners' needs are met. This reflects the Shia scholarly view that true strength lies in attentiveness to the rights and feelings of others.
